title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Cardioactive steroid toxicity results from excessive exposure to cardiac glycosides such as digoxin or plant-derived toxins, including oleander and foxglove. These agents inhibit the Na + , K + -ATPase pump, leading to increased intracellular calcium, impaired sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction, and increased myocardial automaticity. Toxicity can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, neurologic changes, electrolyte disturbances, and life-threatening arrhythmias, requiring prompt recognition and coordinated management.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity, designed for healthcare professionals, is designed to strengthen the learner’s ability to recognize cardioactive steroid toxicity. Participants will enhance their skills in interpreting diagnostic findings and initiating timely, appropriate treatment. This activity also emphasizes the importance of effective interprofessional collaboration to support prevention strategies, enhance patient safety, improve clinical outcomes, and promote optimal team performance.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Identify the clinical signs, symptoms, and electrocardiographic findings of cardioactive steroid toxicity. Implement appropriate monitoring and initial stabilization in patients with suspected cardioactive steroid toxicity. Apply evidence-based management of cardioactive steroid toxicity, including the timely use of digoxin-specific antibody fragments. Coordinate interprofessional care of cardioactive steroid toxicity, including monitoring, antidote administration, patient education, and follow-up, to improve patient safety, clinical outcomes, and prevention of recurrent toxicity. title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Introduction
content: Cardioactive steroids (CAS), also known as cardiac glycosides, are pharmacologically active compounds that have been used for centuries to treat heart failure and edema, historically referred to as “dropsy.” Therapeutic use dates back to the 18th century, when William Withering described the effects of foxglove ( Digitalis purpurea ). These compounds occur naturally in several plants, including oleander ( Nerium oleander) , foxglove ( Digitalis species), lily of the valley ( Convallaria majalis ), red squill ( Drimia maritima ), dogbane ( Apocynum species), and milkweed ( Asclepias species). Digoxin is primarily derived from Digitalis lanata , whereas Digitalis purpurea contains digitoxin and related glycosides. Some traditional herbal remedies and supplements may also contain CAS and pose a risk of toxicity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Introduction
content: Digoxin is the most widely used CAS in modern medicine and is indicated for symptomatic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and for ventricular rate control in atrial fibrillation. Available in tablet, capsule, and oral solution forms, the capsule formulations demonstrate slightly greater bioavailability. Other, less commonly used CAS include digitoxin, ouabain, deslanoside, and lanatoside C. Historical accounts suggest that Vincent van Gogh’s use of digitalis-containing treatments may have contributed to xanthopsia (yellow visual discoloration), a factor proposed to have influenced the yellow tones in his paintings.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Etiology
content: CAS toxicity, most commonly due to digoxin, occurs in acute and chronic forms. Acute toxicity typically results from intentional overdose, accidental ingestion (particularly in children), dosing errors, or ingestion of plants containing cardioactive glycosides. Chronic toxicity more commonly develops in patients receiving therapeutic digoxin and is often due to impaired renal clearance, drug–drug interactions, electrolyte abnormalities, or changes in volume status that increase serum drug concentrations or tissue sensitivity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Etiology
content: Digoxin is primarily eliminated unchanged by the kidneys, making renal insufficiency the most significant risk factor for chronic digoxin toxicity. Older age also increases risk due to reduced renal function, decreased lean body mass, and altered pharmacokinetics. Drug interactions, including those involving amiodarone, verapamil, quinidine, macrolides, and certain antifungal agents, can increase digoxin levels by reducing renal clearance or inhibiting P-glycoprotein–mediated transport. Electrolyte disturbances, particularly hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypercalcemia, enhance digoxin’s effects at the Na + , K + -ATPase pump and increase susceptibility to toxicity even at therapeutic serum concentrations.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Etiology
content: CAS toxicity may also occur following ingestion of plants or animal products containing cardiac glycosides. Common plant sources include foxglove, oleander, lily of the valley, and red squill. Certain herbal preparations and traditional medicines may contain cardioactive glycosides. [1] [2] [3] Animal-derived toxins, such as bufadienolides found in Bufo bufo (common toad) and Rhinella margaritifera (Amozonian toad) toad secretions and preparations such as Ch'an Su, exert similar pharmacologic effects. [4] [5]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Epidemiology
content: CAS toxicity remains a clinically significant cause of cardiovascular poisoning worldwide. The American Heart Association notes that although prescribing of digoxin and digitoxin has declined in recent decades, toxicity continues to occur due to overdose, unintentional ingestion, drug–drug interactions, and accumulation in patients with impaired renal clearance. Older adults are disproportionately affected due to age-related declines in renal function and polypharmacy. Among patients aged 85 years and older, digoxin toxicity accounts for approximately 3.3% of emergency department visits and 5.9% of hospitalizations related to adverse drug events. [6] [7]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Epidemiology
content: Analysis of U.S. surveillance data from 2005 to 2010 estimated approximately 5,156 emergency department visits annually for digoxin toxicity, with 78.8% resulting in hospitalization. Notably, rates of emergency department visits and hospitalizations remained relatively stable during this period despite declining digoxin prescribing, suggesting that toxicity risk persists among exposed patients. [8]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Epidemiology
content: CAS toxicity from herbal supplements and traditional medicines is increasingly recognized. Toxicity may result from intrinsic CAS content, contamination, adulteration, or misidentification of plant materials. Plant-derived poisoning remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in certain regions. Yellow oleander ( Thevetia peruviana ) poisoning is particularly prevalent in South Asia, including India and Sri Lanka, where it represents a common method of intentional self-poisoning and is associated with substantial mortality. [9] [10] Animal-derived CAS, such as bufadienolides found in Bufo toad secretions used in traditional remedies and aphrodisiacs, can also cause life-threatening cardiac toxicity. [10]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Epidemiology
content: The true incidence of supplement-related CAS toxicity is likely underreported due to incomplete exposure histories, inconsistent supplement regulation, and limitations of standard immunoassays, which may not detect all CAS compounds. Clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for CAS toxicity in patients presenting with unexplained arrhythmias, particularly in the setting of renal impairment, polypharmacy, or herbal supplement use.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Pathophysiology
content: The chemical structure of a CAS contains a steroid nucleus and a 5- or 6-membered lactone ring. Cardenolides, which are 5-membered rings, are mostly from plants, while bufadienolides, containing a 6-membered ring, are primarily animal-based. [11] Digitoxin and digoxin, which originate from foxglove, belong to the cardenolide class, whereas bufadienolides such as bufalin originate from mammals, amphibians, certain insects (eg, lightning bugs of the Photinus species), and plant sources such as red squill. [12]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Pathophysiology
content: CAS primarily serve as inotropic agents in therapeutic settings. In addition to myocytes, they affect vascular smooth muscle and the sympathetic nervous system. Their primary mechanism of action is the reversible inhibition of the Na + , K + -ATPase, which increases intracellular sodium and decreases intracellular potassium, thereby inactivating the sodium-calcium antiporter and causing intracellular calcium accumulation. This accumulation of intracellular calcium triggers further calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, ultimately increasing myocardial contractility. In addition to increasing inotropy, CAS increases vagal tone in the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, thereby decreasing conduction and shortening the refractory period, which increases the risk of automaticity and arrhythmias.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Toxicokinetics
content: Digoxin and digitoxin (not available in the United States) are the 2 primary CAS used clinically. They differ significantly in their pharmacokinetics. Digitoxin has higher oral bioavailability and greater protein binding (approximately 90%-95%). In contrast, digoxin is less protein-bound (20%-30%) but has a larger volume of distribution due to extensive tissue binding, particularly in skeletal muscle. Digitoxin undergoes predominantly hepatic metabolism and biliary excretion. In contrast, digoxin is eliminated primarily by renal excretion. [13] As a result, renal impairment significantly increases the risk of digoxin toxicity, while digitoxin toxicity is less affected by kidney function.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Toxicokinetics
content: Both drugs have a narrow therapeutic index, requiring careful dose adjustment based on renal function (digoxin), age, drug interactions, and electrolyte status. Several medications increase digoxin levels by reducing renal clearance or altering distribution, including quinidine, amiodarone, verapamil, diltiazem, spironolactone, and carvedilol.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Toxicokinetics
content: The intestinal bacterium Eggerthella lenta (formerly Eubacterium lentum ) metabolizes digoxin into inactive compounds in some individuals, reducing drug bioavailability. Antibiotics that suppress this bacterium may increase digoxin absorption and serum concentrations, thereby increasing the risk of toxicity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- History and Physical
content: CAS toxicity presents with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations involving the cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurologic, and visual systems. Symptoms vary depending on whether toxicity is acute or chronic and may be nonspecific, particularly in older adults receiving chronic therapy.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- History and Physical -- History
content: Patients with acute CAS toxicity often present within hours of ingestion, commonly due to intentional overdose, accidental ingestion, or consumption of plant- or animal-derived CAS. Early symptoms frequently include gastrointestinal complaints such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and anorexia. Neurologic symptoms, including fatigue, weakness, dizziness, and confusion, may follow.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- History and Physical -- History
content: Chronic CAS toxicity typically develops gradually and often occurs in older adults receiving therapeutic digoxin, particularly in the setting of renal impairment, dehydration, electrolyte abnormalities, or drug interactions. Patients may present with vague symptoms such as fatigue, lethargy, anorexia, nausea, confusion, or functional decline. Visual disturbances, including blurred vision, diplopia, photophobia, scotomas, and color vision abnormalities such as xanthopsia, are characteristic and may suggest chronic toxicity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- History and Physical -- History
content: Clinicians should obtain a thorough medication history, including prescription drugs, herbal supplements, and potential exposure to plant-derived CAS such as foxglove or oleander. A history of renal disease, recent illness, dehydration, or medication changes increases the risk of toxicity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: Vital sign abnormalities are common. Bradycardia due to increased vagal tone and atrioventricular nodal suppression is a frequent finding. Hypotension may occur in severe cases. General examination findings may include lethargy, confusion, or altered mental status, particularly in chronic toxicity. Signs of dehydration, such as dry mucous membranes or decreased skin turgor, may be present, increasing the risk of toxicity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
content: In addition to bradycardia and arrhythmia, the cardiovascular examination may reveal signs of reduced cardiac output. Severe toxicity may result in syncope or signs of hemodynamic instability. Neurologic examination may demonstrate confusion, delirium, or visual disturbances. Visual symptoms are often subjective but can be important diagnostic clues.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Evaluation
content: In acute ingestion, the clinician should obtain digoxin or digitoxin levels at presentation and at least 6 hours after ingestion. Given the distribution phase, levels 6 hours post-ingestion better correlate with digoxin effects. For patients suspected of chronic toxicity, 1 level should suffice. Experts consider levels above 2 ng/ml for digoxin and above 40 ng/ml for digitoxin 6 hours after the last dose to be clinically toxic.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Evaluation
content: Clinicians should monitor electrolytes soon after presentation, as hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypercalcemia increase susceptibility to the toxic cardiac effects of digoxin. Hyperkalemia correlates with mortality. Studies indicate that serum potassium levels above 5.5 mEq/L are associated with significantly increased mortality. [14] Assessment of renal function is of paramount importance given the renal clearance of digoxin. Patients suspected of intentional ingestion should also undergo an assessment of acetaminophen and salicylate levels to assess for possible co-ingestants. Patients who can get pregnant and are of childbearing age should undergo pregnancy testing, and a fingerstick glucose level is necessary to exclude hypoglycemia as a potential cause of altered mental status.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Evaluation
content: Serial ECGs and continuous cardiac monitoring are necessary to detect arrhythmias. Clinicians should be aware that chronic digoxin therapy produces characteristic ECG changes, including scooped ST-segment depression, T-wave flattening or inversion, shortened QT interval, and prominent U waves, that reflect therapeutic effects rather than toxicity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Evaluation
content: Given the CAS mechanism of action, virtually any arrhythmia may occur, although the combination of bradyarrhythmias or AV block with concurrent ventricular ectopy or tachyarrhythmias is highly suggestive of CAS toxicity. [15] Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia, characterized by beat-to-beat alternation in QRS axis, is considered nearly pathognomonic. However, it may rarely occur in aconitine toxicity and in catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia. [16] [17] Younger individuals are more commonly affected by vagally mediated bradyarrhythmias. In contrast, patients with underlying structural heart disease are at greater risk of ventricular dysrhythmias.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Treatment / Management -- Gastrointestinal Decontamination
content: Initial management of CAS toxicity follows standard toxicologic principles, including stabilization of airway, breathing, and circulation. Because digoxin is rapidly absorbed, clinicians may consider gastrointestinal decontamination with activated charcoal if the patient presents early, particularly within 1 to 2 hours of ingestion. However, the benefit may extend beyond this window due to delayed gastrointestinal transit. Activated charcoal is administered orally at a dose of 1 g/kg. Multidose activated charcoal may be used in severe poisoning, particularly with digitoxin, to interrupt enterohepatic recirculation. Though rarely used in clinical practice, cholestyramine and colestipol may also reduce gastrointestinal reabsorption.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Treatment / Management -- Antidotal therapy with Digoxin-Specific Antibody Fragments
content: Definitive treatment involves administration of digoxin-specific antibody fragments (digoxin immune Fab), which bind free digoxin and reverse its toxic effects. Indications include life-threatening arrhythmias, potassium greater than 5.0 to 5.5 mEq/L in acute toxicity, hemodynamic instability or end-organ dysfunction attributable to toxicity, symptomatic chronic toxicity with arrhythmias or neurologic symptoms, acute ingestion with digoxin concentration above 10 ng/mL at 6 or more hours post ingestion, or suspected toxicity from non-digoxin CAS such as oleander. Asymptomatic patients with mildly elevated digoxin levels generally do not require Fab therapy. [18]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Treatment / Management -- Antidotal therapy with Digoxin-Specific Antibody Fragments
content: One vial of digoxin immune Fab binds approximately 0.5 mg of digoxin. Clinicians calculate digoxin immune Fab dosing based on the amount ingested, the serum digoxin concentration, or empiric dosing when these data are unavailable or plant-derived CAS ingestion is suspected. Serum digoxin concentrations do not reliably reflect the severity of toxicity from naturally occurring CAS.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Treatment / Management -- Antidotal therapy with Digoxin-Specific Antibody Fragments
content: If neither the quantity ingested nor the digoxin levels are available, an empiric dose of 10 vials of digoxin immune Fab is an option. In children, 5 vials are permissible. In very small children, clinicians must be cautious of volume overload. If the quantity ingested is known but not the digoxin level, clinicians may calculate the necessary number of vials using the following formula: Number of vials = Dose ingested (in mg) x 1.6 If the levels of digoxin are known, then the number of vials to give is derived by the following formula: Number of vials = (serum digoxin concentration in ng/mL) x (patient's weight in kg)/100 An empiric dose of 10 vials in adults and 5 vials in children is appropriate for severe toxicity.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Treatment / Management -- General Management
content: Hyperkalemia is a marker of severe toxicity and typically corrects rapidly following Fab administration as Na + , K + -ATPase function recovers and potassium shifts intracellularly. Routine aggressive potassium-lowering therapy is generally unnecessary and may increase the risk of hypokalemia after Fab administration. Calcium administration, once avoided due to concerns about worsening toxicity, is no longer considered contraindicated when clinically indicated; however, Fab therapy remains the definitive treatment. [19] [20] [21] [22] [23] Clinicians should promptly correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia to reduce the risk of arrhythmias.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Treatment / Management -- General Management
content: Supportive management includes administering atropine for symptomatic bradycardia, providing intravenous fluids to treat hypotension and improve renal perfusion, and using lidocaine or phenytoin to manage ventricular arrhythmias. Clinicians should avoid antiarrhythmics that worsen atrioventricular conduction or increase digoxin levels, such as amiodarone and procainamide. Continuous cardiac monitoring is required. Clinicians should not use digoxin levels to guide management after Fab administration because assays detect both free and Fab-bound digoxin. Patients with symptomatic toxicity require hospital admission, and those with severe arrhythmias or hemodynamic instability require intensive care monitoring.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Toxicologic and non-toxicologic conditions can mimic digoxin toxicity. Toxicologic mimics include calcium channel blockers, ß-blockers, and clonidine overdose, which may cause bradycardia and hypotension. Hyperglycemia supports calcium channel blocker overdose, whereas clonidine toxicity more commonly produces CNS and respiratory depression with miosis; however, these features are not sufficient to exclude digoxin toxicity. Non-toxicologic mimics include hypothermia, hypothyroidism, myocardial infarction, sinus node dysfunction (including sick sinus syndrome), and hyperkalemia.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Interpretation of serum digoxin concentrations requires caution, as plant-derived CAS can cause digoxin-like toxicity; however, standard digoxin assays may be unreliable, and exposure may not be recognized immediately. Additionally, endogenous digoxin-like immunoreactive substances (DLIS) in volume-expanded states (eg, uremia and renal failure, liver disease, and preeclampsia) and certain exogenous agents (eg, spironolactone, canrenone, potassium canrenoate, and some traditional herbal preparations) may cross-react with some digoxin immunoassays, falsely elevating results. When clinically necessary and available, measuring free digoxin in protein-free ultrafiltrate can reduce interference from protein-bound digoxin.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Prognosis
content: The prognosis of CAS toxicity varies substantially based on the source of exposure, severity of presentation, and access to specific antidotal therapy. However, overall survival can be favorable with appropriate treatment, particularly when digoxin-specific Fab antibodies are available. For digoxin and digitoxin poisoning, observational studies show response rates of 50% to 90% after digoxin-Fab administration, with dysrhythmia resolution typically occurring within 30 to 45 minutes. [7] An observational study among patients presenting in cardiac arrest from digoxin toxicity reports survival rates of 54% in patients treated with digoxin-Fab. [7] [24]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Prognosis
content: Acute accidental poisoning from plants containing cardiac glycosides (lily of the valley, oleander, and foxglove) is common due to their narrow therapeutic index. [25] Death occurs from ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia. [26] The prognosis depends heavily on access to digoxin immune Fab, which may be limited in resource-poor countries where plant-based poisoning is more prevalent.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Prognosis
content: Hyperkalemia is a critical prognostic marker in acute CAS toxicity and reflects the severity of Na + , K + -ATPase inhibition. Higher potassium levels correlate with increased risk of life-threatening arrhythmias and mortality. Historically, potassium levels greater than 5.5 mEq/L were associated with very high mortality rates in untreated patients; however, the availability of digoxin-specific antibody fragments has dramatically improved survival. Hyperkalemia serves primarily as a marker of severe toxicity rather than the direct cause of death, and correction of serum potassium alone does not reverse toxicity. Definitive treatment requires administration of digoxin immune Fab to neutralize circulating toxin and restore cellular ion homeostasis. [14] Patients who present with chronic digoxin toxicity and remain untreated have a mortality ranging from 5% to 13%. [27]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Complications
content: Clinicians must maintain vigilance for cardiac arrhythmias and electrolyte abnormalities in patients with CAS toxicity. These agents produce a characteristic combination of impaired atrioventricular nodal conduction, attributable to increased vagal tone, and increased myocardial automaticity, attributable to intracellular calcium accumulation, thereby allowing virtually any type of arrhythmia to occur. Hyperkalemia reflects severe toxicity. Patients may also develop neurologic symptoms such as confusion, weakness, or altered mental status, most often secondary to cerebral hypoperfusion caused by arrhythmias and reduced cardiac output. In rare cases, severe hypoperfusion may result in end-organ ischemia, including mesenteric ischemia. [28]

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: CAS toxicity results from excessive exposure to cardiac glycosides, including prescription medications such as digoxin and plant-derived toxins found in oleander, foxglove, and lily of the valley. These agents inhibit the Na + , K + -ATPase pump, increasing intracellular calcium, enhancing myocardial contractility, and slowing sinoatrial and atrioventricular conduction. Although digoxin remains clinically useful for select patients with atrial fibrillation and heart failure, its narrow therapeutic index increases the risk of toxicity, particularly in older adults, patients with renal impairment, and those receiving interacting medications. CAS toxicity may present with gastrointestinal symptoms, visual disturbances, neurologic changes, and life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Healthcare professionals play a critical role in preventing CAS toxicity through appropriate prescribing, patient education, and monitoring. Clinicians should prescribe the lowest effective dose and adjust dosing based on renal function, age, body mass, and clinical indication. Regular assessment of renal function and electrolyte status, particularly potassium, calcium, and magnesium, and review of concomitant medications are essential, as hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and drug interactions significantly increase the risk of toxicity. Medications that increase serum digoxin concentrations, including amiodarone, verapamil, diltiazem, quinidine, macrolide antibiotics, and certain antifungals, require dose adjustment or closer monitoring.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patient education should emphasize strict adherence to prescribed dosing and avoidance of double-dosing if they miss a dose. Clinicians should instruct patients to recognize early symptoms of toxicity, including nausea, vomiting, fatigue, visual disturbances (eg, blurred or yellow vision), palpitations, dizziness, or syncope, and to seek prompt medical attention if these symptoms occur. Patients should also inform healthcare professionals of all medications, supplements, and herbal products they use, as certain herbal preparations and plant exposures may contain cardioactive steroids or interfere with digoxin metabolism or laboratory assays.Healthcare professionals should counsel patients to avoid ingestion of unknown plants, herbal remedies, or teas, particularly those containing oleander, foxglove, or other cardiac glycoside–containing plants. Caregivers and family members should also be educated about the importance of secure medication storage to prevent accidental ingestion, especially in children and older adults with cognitive impairment.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Physicians and advanced practitioners, including nurse practitioners and physician assistants, play a central role in identifying patients at risk, recognizing early signs of toxicity, and initiating appropriate evaluation and treatment. These clinicians must assess clinical presentation, review medication history, identify contributing factors such as renal dysfunction or drug interactions, and determine the need for interventions, including electrolyte correction, antiarrhythmic therapy, or administration of digoxin-specific antibody fragments. They are also responsible for ensuring appropriate monitoring, adjusting medication dosing based on renal function and clinical response, and coordinating specialty consultations when necessary, including cardiology, toxicology, or nephrology.

title: Cardioactive Steroid Toxicity -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Pharmacists play a critical role in preventing CAS toxicity by reviewing medication regimens for drug interactions, recommending appropriate dosing adjustments, and assisting with therapeutic drug monitoring. Pharmacists also help identify medications that increase digoxin concentrations, such as amiodarone, verapamil, macrolide antibiotics, and certain antifungals, and guide dose modifications or alternative therapies. During acute toxicity, pharmacists assist in calculating the appropriate dosing of digoxin immune Fab and help ensure timely access to this antidote.

content: Nurses are essential for continuous patient monitoring and early detection of clinical deterioration. Nurses also provide patient education regarding medication adherence, symptom recognition, and prevention strategies.
